draft.title: Quartiles and interquartile range
card: Put the data in order. The quartiles split the ordered data into four parts, with about the same number of values in each.
The median splits the ordered data into a lower half and an upper half. If there is an odd number of values, leave the median out of both halves.
\(Q_{1}\) is the median of the lower half. \(Q_{3}\) is the median of the upper half. The interquartile range is \(\text{IQR} = Q_{3} - Q_{1}\), the spread of the middle half of the data.
draft.remember: Order first, split at the median, then \(\text{IQR} = Q_{3} - Q_{1}\).

a.q: Last term, seven students each read this many books: 4, 9, 2, 7, 5, 11, 6. What is the IQR?
a.why: In order the data is 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 11. The median is 6, \(Q_{1}\) is 4 and \(Q_{3}\) is 9, so \(\text{IQR} = 9 - 4 = 5\). Using 9 is tempting, but that is the range (\(11 - 2\)), not a spread found from the quartiles.
a.clue: Put the values in order before you find any quartile.

b.q: Waiting times at a Bendigo clinic, in minutes, are 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 20. Find the IQR.
b.why: There are 8 values, so the lower half is 3, 5, 6, 8 and the upper half is 10, 12, 15, 20. \(Q_{1} = 5.5\) and \(Q_{3} = 13.5\), so \(\text{IQR} = 13.5 - 5.5 = 8\). The value 13.5 is only \(Q_{3}\), and 17 is the range.
b.clue: With 8 values, split into two halves of 4 and find the middle of each.
